name: plog
listed_description: Portable and simple log for C++ in less than 1000 lines of code.
reason: README Performance section gives only absolute microseconds per log call on five old CPUs (8 to 68 microsec: Phenom II 1055T, Core i3-3120M, Core i5-2500K, Atom N270) with no comparison against any other logger or std::cerr, and states plog is not asynchronous and may slow an application at high volume. Not in the reckless performance.md, MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark or RafaGago/logger-bench READMEs (all fetched, no plog row), and not in spdlog's README benchmark tables (the spdlog bench directory once had plog-bench targets, but no published plog numbers were found). Changelog '9% on Windows' is plog against its own older version. Four WebSearch queries found no third-party plog numbers.

name: pthreads
listed_description: POSIX thread library. Standard (no license applicable).
reason: A standard API (IEEE 1003.1c), not a repository or one implementation, with no licence and no code to catalog. The Wikipedia page could not be opened (en.wikipedia.org egress blocked: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so no numeric comparison was reachable. The only known numbers belong to specific implementations (for example the NPTL design paper against LinuxThreads), which would be a separate glibc/NPTL entry and need a source that is blocked here (akkadia.org not tried).

name: Quantum
listed_description: A powerful C++ coroutine dispatcher framework built on top of Boost.Coroutine2.
reason: README, wiki page 1. Introduction and repo tree (docs, cmake, quantum, tests; no benchmark directory) carry only qualitative claims: 'Highly parallelized coroutine framework for CPU-bound workloads', 'Fast pre-allocated memory pools', 'extremely cheap' context switches, 'streaming futures ... faster processing of large data sets'. No numbers and no named baseline. One WebSearch found no third-party benchmark (tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks does not include Quantum). Directional claim, no numbers, so no record.

name: RaftLib
listed_description: The RaftLib C++ library, streaming/dataflow concurrency via C++ iostream-like operators.
reason: Repo page and README (fetched) carry no benchmark numbers: BUILD_BENCHMARKS defaults to false and the README calls the benchmark collection 'a work in progress'. The separate repo https://github.com/RaftLib/benchmarks (PARSEC streamcluster, fluidanimate, parallel-bzip) has no results either. A peer-reviewed paper exists (Beard, Li, Chamberlain, 'RaftLib: A C++ Template Library for High Performance Stream Parallel Processing', PMAM 2015 and IJHPCA 2016) whose string-search evaluation compares RaftLib Aho-Corasick/Boyer-Moore-Horspool against GNU Parallel with grep and Apache Spark (search snippets say near-linear scaling to 16 cores; one garbled snippet suggests RaftLib is roughly 1.5 GB/s against Spark roughly 2.8 GB/s, unverified). Every host with the PDF or numbers was egress blocked (raftlib.io, www.ccrc.wustl.edu, arxiv.org, openscholarship.wustl.edu, static.aminer.org, acawiki.org, researchgate), so no number could be opened. Worth a retry from a thread with paper access (likely tier B, direction possibly not faster than Spark).

name: Remotery
listed_description: Single C File Profiler with Web Viewer.
reason: README (readme.md, fetched) has one number: the web viewer's 'GPU UI rendering, bypassing the DOM completely, for real-time 60hz viewer updates at 10,000x the performance'. That compares Remotery's own new viewer against its own earlier DOM-based UI, with no workload, method or named recognizable baseline profiler. No profiling-overhead figures and no comparison against Tracy, Optick, MicroProfile or perf anywhere in the repo page; one WebSearch for Remotery against Tracy/Optick overhead found none (only a qualitative 'very low' compile-time rating from a blog). No record.

name: rotor
listed_description: Event loop friendly C++ actor micro framework.
reason: README 'messaging performance' table gives only rotor's own absolute throughput (~31.6M msgs/s inter-thread, ~2.5M msgs/s cross-thread, ~49.6M single thread, ~34.9M and ~71.33M no-alloc) on an Intel Core i7-1360P under Void Linux, with no other actor framework or std facility as comparison. SObjectizer appears only as an inspiration; CAF is not mentioned. Changelog 'up to 15% / +20%' claims compare rotor against its own earlier versions. No benchmark directory; one WebSearch found no third-party rotor against SObjectizer/CAF benchmark.

name: SaneCppLibraries
listed_description: A set of C++ platform abstraction libraries for macOS, Windows and Linux.
reason: README and Documentation/Pages/Principles.md list 'Fast compile times' and 'Bloat free' as principles with no measurements. Support/Benchmarks/Http README describes a tool comparing AsyncWebServer with Python's built-in HTTP server, but its numbers (71.01 vs 45.23 requests/sec) are a placeholder 'Example Output' block (AsyncWebServer built in Debug in the instructions), not a measured result. FAQ mentions Support/Scripts/BenchmarkStdCppMode.sh (normal against strict build, 'not a CI performance threshold'), self against self. No comparison with libuv, std::filesystem or others found; one WebSearch for compile-time comparisons found nothing.
